client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time there's a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — I see his empty chair or someone mentions something he used to do, and I completely fall apart. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the grief is just... there, you know?
therapist: What you're carrying sounds so heavy, and it makes complete sense that those moments at family gatherings bring the grief rushing back so vividly — grief has a way of living in the details, like an empty chair. You're right that talking won't make it disappear, but sometimes it can help us find a little more room to breathe alongside it, rather than being completely swept away. I'm wondering — when you "fall apart" in those moments, what kinds of thoughts tend to go through your mind?

client: When I fall apart, the main thought that hits me is that I should have been there more before he died — like I wasted so much time on stupid arguments and being too busy, and now I can never fix that. And then I feel this crushing guilt on top of the grief, like I don't even deserve to be sad because some of it was my own fault. It's hard to even sit with those thoughts long enough to examine them, because they feel so true and so final.
therapist: That guilt layered on top of grief sounds absolutely exhausting — like you're not even allowing yourself the comfort of mourning because part of you is using the pain as a punishment. I want to gently notice something: the fact that you *care* this much about the lost time actually speaks to how deeply you loved him, not to a failure on your part — complicated relationships are part of almost every close bond. Can you tell me a little about a moment, even a small one, where you *were* there for your dad in a way that mattered?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I want to believe it, but my brain keeps pushing back on it. Like, yes, I can think of moments... there was this one time he was in the hospital a few years back and I drove three hours in the middle of the night to be there. But then my mind immediately goes to "well, that was just one time, and what about all the times you didn't show up?" It's like I can't let the good moments just be good moments without immediately countering them.
therapist: That pattern you're describing — where your mind immediately discounts the good evidence and hunts for the negative — is actually a really well-known thinking trap called "mental filtering," and noticing it so clearly is genuinely significant. That three-hour drive in the middle of the night isn't a small thing; it's the kind of act that reveals who you are to someone you love. I'm curious — if a close friend described their relationship with their father the exact same way you've described yours, would you tell them they didn't deserve to grieve?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them their feelings made complete sense. But it's different when it's me — I just keep thinking I should have done more, called more, visited more, and now there's no chance to fix any of it.
therapist: You just noticed something really important — that you hold yourself to a completely different standard than you'd hold someone you love, and that gap is worth sitting with. The "should haves" feel so loud right now, but they're built on the assumption that you weren't doing your best with what you had at the time — the busyness, the arguments, all of it happened in a context. What do you think was going on in your life or in that relationship that made it hard to show up in the ways you're now wishing you had?

client: I guess... there was just so much going on at that time. I was stressed about work constantly, and every time we tried to talk it would spiral into this argument where we'd both just shut down. I think I kept telling myself I'd make more time when things settled down, but they never really did, and now that feels like such a stupid excuse.
therapist: What you're describing doesn't sound like a stupid excuse — it sounds like a very human person caught between real pressures, hoping for a future window that never came, which is something so many people experience without ever expecting to face this kind of ending. There's a difference between a choice made out of not caring and a pattern that developed because life was genuinely hard and the relationship had its own painful dynamics that made connection difficult. I'm wondering — do you think your dad, knowing everything about your life and the struggles between you two, would have seen it as you simply not caring enough?

client: I want to say no, that he would have understood... but honestly, I'm not sure. We had this distance between us for so long that I don't even know if he knew the full picture of what my life was like. And that's almost worse, you know? That he might have just thought I didn't care, because I never actually told him how overwhelmed I was.
therapist: That particular ache — wondering if he truly knew you, and fearing he might have misread your absence as indifference — sounds like one of the most painful parts of this whole loss. It points to something really tender: not just grief for him, but grief for the version of the relationship where you both fully understood each other. I'm curious — is there anything you wish you could have told him about your life or yourself that he didn't get to hear?

client: Yeah, there's... there's actually a lot I wish he could have known. I think I wanted him to understand that I wasn't pulling away because I didn't care — I was just so caught up in my own struggles, my anxiety, always feeling like I wasn't handling things well enough to show up properly. I guess I kept waiting until I had it more together before reconnecting, and that moment never came.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — you weren't withholding yourself out of indifference, you were waiting until you felt *worthy* of showing up, and that waiting came from a place of anxiety and self-doubt, not a lack of love. That's a very different story than the one your guilt has been telling you. I wonder if that same pattern — waiting until you feel "together enough" before allowing yourself connection or comfort — might also be part of what makes grieving feel so hard to sit with right now?

client: Yeah, I think you're onto something, but it also makes me feel kind of sick to hear it laid out like that. Like, if I've been keeping myself at a distance until I felt "ready," then I missed so much time with him that I can never get back. And now I'm supposed to just... sit with that grief without running from it, but honestly I don't even know what that looks like.
therapist: That realization landing so heavily makes complete sense — it's painful to see a pattern clearly, because clarity can briefly feel like a verdict before it starts to feel like freedom. Sitting with grief doesn't mean forcing yourself to feel everything all at once; it often starts with something much smaller, like letting yourself have one memory of him without immediately following it with a "but." What do you think it would feel like to let that hospital drive — that three-hour midnight journey — just exist as a true expression of your love, without your mind adding a "however" after it?

client: I want to let that drive just be what it was, but my mind almost immediately goes to "yeah, but he never acknowledged it, he never even said thank you." It's like I can hold the love for maybe two seconds before the resentment rushes in and takes over, and then I feel guilty for the resentment, which makes everything worse. I don't know if I'm capable of separating those two things right now.
therapist: What you're describing — love and resentment tangled so tightly together that you can barely touch one without the other rushing in — is actually a sign of how real and complex this relationship was, not a sign that something is broken in you. The resentment doesn't cancel the love, and feeling it doesn't make you a bad son; it makes you someone who wanted more from a relationship that didn't always give back in the ways you needed. I'm wondering — do you think that unacknowledged drive, and maybe other moments like it, left you carrying a loneliness in that relationship that you've never really had space to grieve alongside the loss itself?

client: Yeah... I think that's probably true, but it's hard to sit with because it feels like I'm admitting the relationship was broken, and I don't want it to be broken. There was this loneliness, yeah, like I was always just slightly out of reach of really being known by him, and I kept thinking if I just tried harder or did more, maybe that would change. I never really let myself grieve that part because it felt disloyal, like I was betraying him by admitting it wasn't enough.
therapist: What you just named takes real courage — that quiet, aching loneliness of being almost known by someone you loved, and the exhausting hope that if you just did a little more, the gap might finally close. Grieving that doesn't betray him; it actually honors the truth of who you both were and what you genuinely longed for together. I want to gently offer that holding the relationship as both real and imperfect, both loving and painful, might actually be the only way to carry it without it crushing you — does any part of you sense that those two things, loving him and grieving what wasn't there, might be allowed to coexist?
